keyVerseText: But the Jews which believed not, moved with envy, took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar, and assaulted the house of Jason, and sought to bring them out to the people.
rootMeaning: The name Ἰάσων (Iásōn) derives from the future active participle masculine form of the Greek verb ἰάομαι (iáomai), which means 'to heal' or 'to make whole.' This etymology highlights a sense of one who is 'about to cure' or 'a healer,' indicating a proactive, ongoing action of restoration. Beyond the common English transliteration 'Jason,' the root sense conveys a deeper spiritual implication of healing and wholeness, which enriches the understanding of the name within a biblical context.
usageInScripture: The word Ἰάσων appears five times in the New Testament, primarily translated as 'Jason' in four occurrences, with one instance as 'of Jason.' This consistent use as a proper name identifies a Christian individual known in the early church, as seen in Acts 17:5-7, 9 and possibly in Romans 16:21. The limited variation in translation underscores the name's function as a personal identifier rather than a common noun, yet its root meaning subtly informs the character and witness of the person named.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Ἰάσων as 'he who is about to heal' enriches the Christian appreciation of personal names in Scripture, revealing God's providence even in the naming of believers. The connection to healing echoes the ministry of Christ, the ultimate healer and restorer of humanity. Recognizing Jason as a Christian bearing a name rooted in healing invites reflection on the believer's role in the body of Christ—to participate in spiritual restoration and wholeness. This insight encourages faithfulness in witnessing and serving, embodying Christ’s healing power in the community of believers.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 17:5 describes an uproar involving the house of Jason, a believer whose home became a refuge for early Christians. The use of the name Ἰάσων here reminds readers that Jason was not only a person but symbolically one associated with healing and restoration. The opposition he faced highlights the spiritual conflict surrounding the gospel, yet his name points to the hope of healing amid persecution. This verse invites believers to trust in God’s healing purposes even when challenged by hostility.
